expectedText:
POST-OFFER, PRE-EMPLOYMENT MEDICAL EXAMINATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Innovations LLC

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes federal and California law governing when Acme Innovations LLC may require Jordan Lee, as a job applicant, to undergo a medical examination or answer disability-related medical questions during the hiring process. It states facts about what the Americans with Disabilities Act, its implementing federal regulation, and California's Fair Employment and Housing Act permit, require, and restrict in this area. It is not itself a medical examination, a consent form, or an authorization for any specific examination, and it does not tell Acme Innovations LLC or Jordan Lee what to do about any particular hiring decision.

BEFORE A JOB OFFER: NO MEDICAL EXAMS OR DISABILITY INQUIRIES
Before Acme Innovations LLC extends a conditional job offer, federal law prohibits it from conducting a medical examination of Jordan Lee or asking whether Jordan Lee has a disability or about the nature or severity of a disability. California law separately prohibits requiring a medical or psychological examination, making a medical or psychological inquiry, or asking whether an applicant has a mental disability, physical disability, or medical condition, at the pre-offer stage. Both laws permit one specific kind of pre-offer question during this stage: Acme Innovations LLC may ask about Jordan Lee's ability to perform job-related functions, and may ask Jordan Lee to describe or demonstrate how those functions would be performed, with or without reasonable accommodation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "a covered entity shall not conduct a medical examination or make inquiries of a job applicant as to whether such applicant is an individual with a disability or as to the nature or severity of such disability"
  — 42 U.S.C. § 12112(d)(2)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Americans with Disabilities Act, pre-offer prohibition (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/12112)
  "A covered entity may make preemployment inquiries into the ability of an applicant to perform job-related functions."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 12112(d)(2)(B) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Americans with Disabilities Act, acceptable pre-offer inquiry (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/12112)
  "A covered entity may make pre-employment inquiries into the ability of an applicant to perform job-related functions, and/or may ask an applicant to describe or to demonstrate how, with or without reasonable accommodation, the applicant will be able to perform job-related functions."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 1630.14(a) (Cornell LII / e-CFR text), EEOC ADA regulation, acceptable pre-employment inquiry (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XIV/part-1630/section-1630.14)
  "for any employer or employment agency to require any medical or psychological examination of an applicant, to make any medical or psychological inquiry of an applicant, to make any inquiry whether an applicant has a mental disability or physical disability or medical condition, or to make any inquiry regarding the nature or severity of a physical disability, mental disability, or medical condition."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(e)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California FEHA, pre-offer prohibition on medical or psychological examination and inquiry (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  "an employer or employment agency may inquire into the ability of an applicant to perform job-related functions and may respond to an applicant’s request for reasonable accommodation."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(e)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California FEHA, acceptable pre-offer inquiry and accommodation response (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  Known gap: Federal and California law are independent sources here, and each is treated as a source in its own right below. The federal EEOC regulation's description of the acceptable pre-offer inquiry (asking an applicant to describe or demonstrate how job functions would be performed, with or without reasonable accommodation) is more specific than the bare statutory text, which speaks only of inquiries into the ability to perform job-related functions; both are quoted below. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific examination or inquiry, and it does not determine whether a conditional offer has been extended in any given case.

AFTER A CONDITIONAL OFFER: A MEDICAL EXAM MAY BE REQUIRED
After Acme Innovations LLC has extended a conditional offer of employment to Jordan Lee, and before Jordan Lee begins job duties, federal law permits Acme Innovations LLC to require a medical examination and to condition the offer on its results — but only if all entering employees in the same job category are required to undergo the same examination, regardless of disability. California law permits the same thing under a parallel, but not identical, standard: it additionally requires that the examination or inquiry itself be job-related and consistent with business necessity, on top of requiring that all entering employees in the same job classification be subject to the same examination or inquiry.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A covered entity may require a medical examination after an offer of employment has been made to a job applicant and prior to the commencement of the employment duties of such applicant, and may condition an offer of employment on the results of such examination, if— (A) all entering employees are subjected to such an examination regardless of disability;"
  — 42 U.S.C. § 12112(d)(3)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Americans with Disabilities Act, permitted post-offer employment entrance examination (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/12112)
  "A covered entity may require a medical examination (and/or inquiry) after making an offer of employment to a job applicant and before the applicant begins his or her employment duties, and may condition an offer of employment on the results of such examination (and/or inquiry), if all entering employees in the same job category are subjected to such an examination (and/or inquiry) regardless of disability."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 1630.14(b) (Cornell LII / e-CFR text), EEOC ADA regulation, employment entrance examination and same-job-category requirement (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XIV/part-1630/section-1630.14)
  "an employer or employment agency may require a medical or psychological examination or make a medical or psychological inquiry of a job applicant after an employment offer has been made but prior to the commencement of employment duties, provided that the examination or inquiry is job related and consistent with business necessity and that all entering employees in the same job classification are subject to the same examination or inquiry."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(e)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California FEHA, permitted post-offer examination with added job-related/business-necessity requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  Known gap: This is a genuine difference between the two laws, not a restatement of one by the other: the federal statute's own text conditions the post-offer exam only on its being required of all entering employees regardless of disability, without an express job-related/business-necessity requirement for the exam itself (the federal EEOC regulation confirms this — it states that exams conducted under this provision "do not have to be job-related and consistent with business necessity," though any criteria later used to screen someone out because of the results must independently meet that standard); California's statute, by contrast, writes a job-related/business-necessity requirement directly into the authorization for the exam itself. An employer relying on this document should not assume the federal and state standards are interchangeable. Both the federal regulation and the state statute independently use the phrase "same job category" / "same job classification" — a detail the bare federal statutory text doesn't include but the regulation adds. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific examination, and it does not determine whether any particular offer is "conditional" for these purposes.

CONFIDENTIALITY OF MEDICAL EXAMINATION RESULTS
Under federal law, information Acme Innovations LLC obtains about Jordan Lee's medical condition or history through a permitted post-offer examination must be collected and kept on separate forms, kept in separate medical files apart from Jordan Lee's regular personnel file, and treated as a confidential medical record. This confidentiality requirement has three specific, limited exceptions: supervisors and managers may be informed of necessary work restrictions and accommodations, first aid and safety personnel may be informed if the condition might require emergency treatment, and government officials investigating compliance may be given relevant information on request.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "information obtained regarding the medical condition or history of the applicant is collected and maintained on separate forms and in separate medical files and is treated as a confidential medical record, except that— (i) supervisors and managers may be informed regarding necessary restrictions on the work or duties of the employee and necessary accommodations; (ii) first aid and safety personnel may be informed, when appropriate, if the disability might require emergency treatment; and (iii) government officials investigating compliance with this chapter shall be provided relevant information on request"
  — 42 U.S.C. § 12112(d)(3)(B) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Americans with Disabilities Act, confidentiality requirements and exceptions for post-offer exam results (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/12112)
  "Information obtained under paragraph (b) of this section regarding the medical condition or history of the applicant shall be collected and maintained on separate forms and in separate medical files and be treated as a confidential medical record, except that: (i) Supervisors and managers may be informed regarding necessary restrictions on the work or duties of the employee and necessary accommodations; (ii) First aid and safety personnel may be informed, when appropriate, if the disability might require emergency treatment; and (iii) Government officials investigating compliance with this part shall be provided relevant information on request."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 1630.14(b)(1) (Cornell LII / e-CFR text), EEOC ADA regulation, confidentiality requirement for post-offer exam results (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XIV/part-1630/section-1630.14)
  Known gap: The federal statute and its implementing regulation are being treated together here as one connected source on this point, not as independent corroborating sources — the regulation restates the same rule the statute establishes. This document's research did not find a confidentiality provision written into California Government Code § 12940 itself paralleling this federal one; § 12940, as fetched for this document, describes when a pre- or post-offer examination or inquiry is permitted but does not itself impose separate-file or separate-form confidentiality requirements on the results. That does not mean California applicants and employees have no other confidentiality protection for medical information under state law generally — only that this particular statute, the one this document otherwise relies on for the pre-offer/post-offer distinction, does not contain one, and no other California confidentiality statute was researched or verified for purposes of this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific examination, and it does not itself establish or enforce any recordkeeping practice.

IF THE EXAM REVEALS A DISABILITY
A permitted post-offer medical examination does not itself have to be job-related and consistent with business necessity to be lawful under the federal regulation — but if Acme Innovations LLC uses the results to screen Jordan Lee out because of a disability, the specific exclusionary criteria used must be job-related and consistent with business necessity, and the exclusion must hold up even considering whether the essential job functions could be performed with reasonable accommodation. California law reaches a similar substantive result through its disability-discrimination provisions generally: it does not prohibit an employer from refusing to hire, or from discharging, a person with a physical or mental disability or a medical condition if that person, because of the disability or condition, cannot perform the job's essential duties even with reasonable accommodations, or cannot perform them without endangering their own health or safety or the health or safety of others, even with reasonable accommodations.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Medical examinations conducted in accordance with this section do not have to be job-related and consistent with business necessity. However, if certain criteria are used to screen out an employee or employees with disabilities as a result of such an examination or inquiry, the exclusionary criteria must be job-related and consistent with business necessity, and performance of the essential job functions cannot be accomplished with reasonable accommodation as required in this part."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 1630.14(b)(3) (Cornell LII / e-CFR text), EEOC ADA regulation, job-related/business-necessity standard for using post-offer exam results to screen out (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XIV/part-1630/section-1630.14)
  "This part does not prohibit an employer from refusing to hire or discharging an employee with a physical or mental disability, or subject an employer to any legal liability resulting from the refusal to employ or the discharge of an employee with a physical or mental disability, if the employee, because of a physical or mental disability, is unable to perform the employee’s essential duties even with reasonable accommodations, or cannot perform those duties in a manner that would not endanger the employee’s health or safety or the health or safety of others even with reasonable accommodations."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California FEHA, limit on disability-discrimination liability where essential duties cannot be performed even with accommodation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  Known gap: The federal point is drawn from the EEOC's own regulation interpreting the ADA's post-offer-examination provision specifically; the California point is drawn from a general disability-discrimination provision of FEHA rather than a subsection addressed specifically to post-offer examinations, since this document's research did not find a FEHA provision addressing withdrawal of an offer after a post-offer exam as specifically as the federal regulation does. The two are stated as separate, independent sources reaching a similar substantive outcome, not as one confirming the other. Neither source is quoted here as resolving whether accommodating any particular condition is possible, what counts as an undue hardship, or what a specific employer's job-related, business-necessity showing must contain in a specific case — both bodies of law require that showing to be made on the specific facts, which this document does not do. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific decision to withdraw an offer.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate that you have received and reviewed this information sheet.

Applicant / Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________
